title: How Does a Bridging Loan Work?
summary: Explainer article (blog) on the mechanics of a bridging loan. Only the opening portion of the page was surfaced by search [a]. Thesis as summarised by the search tool: a bridging loan is short-term financing that covers the gap between an immediate funding need and a longer-term solution, giving property buyers or investors fast access to capital so they can proceed with a transaction without waiting for a traditional mortgage or a property sale to complete. Concrete guidance revealed: the loan is secured against property and typically repaid over 6 to 24 months; lenders underwrite on the property's value and the borrower's exit plan rather than on income; the first step is an application and valuation at which the lender sets the loan-to-value ratio; the borrower must demonstrate a clear repayment route such as a sale or refinance; rates are generally higher than conventional mortgages and fees can include arrangement, valuation and exit fees. Search [b] (site-wide keyword query) returned a synthesis across several Silver Oak bridging pages, not attributable to this article alone: interest can be paid monthly or retained and settled at the end of the term; exit strategy is often the most scrutinised detail; bridging loans can be granted in a matter of days or weeks; a common use is buying a new home before selling the current one and repaying from the sale proceeds. H1, meta description, headings, FAQ block and calls to action were NOT revealed.

sections.content: [a] Lenders focus on the property's value and the borrower's exit plan rather than income. The first step is an application and valuation, where the lender sets the loan-to-value ratio. The borrower must also show a clear way to repay, such as a sale or refinance.

sections.heading: Context from other Silver Oak bridging pages (NOT this article)
sections.content: [a] One other page says most bridging loans are structured as interest-only products, with interest either serviced monthly or rolled-up and repaid at the end of the loan term; another describes the typical term as between 3 and 24 months. [b] Across several site pages: term usually 6 to 24 months, with another page giving 1 to 36 months and some lenders offering longer; exit strategy is often the most scrutinised detail by lenders; interest can be paid monthly or retained and settled at the end of the term; common costs are arrangement, valuation and exit fees; common use is buying a new home before selling the current one, repaid from the sale proceeds; loans can be granted in a matter of days or weeks.
